title: Television school training and being class producer
summary: Hall describes the coursework and live shows and being class producer without getting hired.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: When I was going to television school, we had genuine instructors. We had our theory part of it in the morning, and then we did studio work in the afternoon five days a week, and I never missed a day.
Towards the end of graduation, the first year -- the first six weeks it was -- there weren't any books written. Nobody knew the formula for doing this thing at that time.
Right.

So the first six weeks you did some of everything. You worked the mikes, the boom -- I mean the boom, the sound and the director's chair and whatnot, floor manager. And then the second half, you specialize in what you're going to do.
The second half of the six weeks?
No, another six weeks.
Six weeks, uh-huh.

So naturally I wanted to be a director, so that's -- that was my specialization at that time. And there was a fellow from Peru, that was a big man in theatrics out there and they sent him to the school so that he could introduce television in Peru.

And naturally he spoke broken English, you know, and sort of a Spanish. The guys used to put him down. And he and I became inseparable. So when I had a show to put on -- we had to put on a show every day. We had a script that was already printed five minutes, ten minutes a show, and then you assume all the different positions you had to have.

So when I was director, he was my assistant, and when he was director, I was his assistant. So we finished the course. I was made class producer. And I introduced live music. I had the show from the Blue Angel, where I was working with Ellis Larkins.
And I introduced the world spinning with the news,
bought a toy map from the confectionary store,
Globe, you mean?

The globe, yeah. And I had a Mickey Mouse comic on it. And I got one demerit in my play. It's called "Duet." And it was a prosty had been out and there was an ashtray full of cigarette butts and whatnot. She's supposed to have a drink.
So all the time we were in rehearsal it's the tea, water, you know. On the final show I got a bottle of scotch.
Yeah, real thin, yeah.
What a tremendous -- what a tremendous shot that was. And it was shown on closed circuit at the General Motors Building at 57th and Broadway. And that's where prospective employers watched the show.

So all the guys, all the cameramen got hired for Shea Stadium -- for Ebbetts Field. Shea wasn't built yet -- for Ebbetts Field. All the other guys in my class got assigned -- we had two guys from Toronto -- CBC. They became major directors.
In Canada.
In Canada. And one of my close buddies became the client's man for Pillsbury. He's still in the job, Wilson Fieldhouse.
(Laughter.)
And I am sending resumes all over the country, but I can't get
ARRESTED
You didn't feel --
But I'm the class producer.
(Laughter.)
You didn't fall into the quotas?
No, there was no quota.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
